patternStatus: Read on 2026-09-09 from the rendered page and from content/patterns/table/table-pattern.html in w3c/aria-practices, so the sentence that decides the family is the source's rather than the page's summary. The itemised comparison is in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-09-table-design.md §2.
roleReason: The pattern's own words: a table "is not an interactive widget. Thus, its cells are not focusable or selectable." Every role the structure needs — table, row, rowgroup, columnheader, rowheader, cell — is what the platform's elements already carry, and writing any of them by hand would restate what the browser states and drift from it.
rootReason: The root is the frame and the scroller is inside it. A sticky header resolves against its nearest scrolling ancestor, which is the scroll part either way; what the root has to hold instead is everything that must not scroll sideways with the table — the border, the radius, the clip, and the footer bar where a paged listing puts its control. Read the other way round, with the root as the scroller, a framed table and its pagination were two boxes with a seam between them, and the consumer had to draw the frame themselves. prose makes the same division for the same reason.

footer.holds: the consumer's own controls under the table and inside its frame: pagination, a page-size select, a count, a bulk-action bar
footer.scrolls: no. It is a sibling of the scroll part rather than a child, so a table scrolled sideways does not take its paging control with it — which is what put the root outside the scroller.
footer.reason: Every surveyed implementation that pages draws the control attached to the table: Carbon and Ant render it themselves, Material puts MatPaginator in the same card. A control floating under a framed box reads as a defect, and the alternative is the consumer drawing the frame themselves and setting the family to plain. The family supplies the place and the rule above it; pagination supplies the control and holds the page.

scroll.wiring: role="region", tabindex="0" and an accessible name, all three written together
scroll.condition: only while the content overflows the scroll part along the inline axis, remeasured by a ResizeObserver, and never under stickyTo page — there the family owns no scroll container, so there is nothing to give a tab stop to
scroll.model: The family scrolls sideways and never up. Vertical scrolling belongs to whatever the consumer gives a height to: the scroll part when they set one on it, and the page when they do not. That is why stickyHeader is off by default — a header fixed inside a box with no height fixes nothing — and why the two axes are separate: stickyHeader says whether the header stays, stickyTo says what it stays inside.
scroll.affordance: the scrollbar, a column visibly cut mid-word at the trailing edge, and a named scrolling region with a tab stop the arrow keys move. A pinned column draws one ordinary rule and no more. It carried a darker line while something was hidden under it — what a spreadsheet does — and read on a real listing that was wrong twice: a table pinning a chooser and the identifier beside it has two seams and only one is a boundary, so the reader was told twice; and the boundary line at the weight the affordance needed read as a wall through a table whose other columns are separated by a hairline. The measurement stays — data-at-start and data-at-end are still written, and a consumer who wants the darker edge has the attributes to draw it.
scroll.reason: The rule prose set, and the one §12 asks for by name: none of the six surveyed implementations leaves a wide table reachable without a pointer, and a tab stop on a table that fits makes the reader press Tab for nothing.

sticky.footer: summary. The totals row is the header of the other end: a listing whose sum, count or unit scrolls out of view makes the reader scroll back for the number they came for, and every surveyed implementation that draws a summary at all pins it — Ant, AG Grid and Material each hold the summary against the bottom of the same box the header is held against the top of. It is the tfoot that is pinned and not the footer bar: the bar is already outside the scroller and never leaves.

to.scroll: The default. The header sticks to the family's own scroller, which is what keeps it correct inside a drawer, a dialog or a split pane — the box the reader is scrolling is the box the header stays in. It needs the scroller to have a height; without one there is nothing to scroll past and nothing to stick to.
to.page: The header sticks to the nearest scrolling ancestor outside the family: the page, an app shell, a scroll area. The family gives up its own scroll container to do it, because a box that scrolls one axis scrolls both — CSS computes a visible axis to auto the moment the other is auto — so a table cannot both scroll sideways inside its frame and let its header stick to the page. What a wide table does in this mode is push the page sideways, or state layout fixed and truncate.
to.offset: --slotted-table-sticky-offset, which is where the header stops. An application with a bar of its own sets it once and every table under it stops below the bar rather than under it.
to.reason: Carbon and Ant stick to the page and Material sticks to its own container; each is right for one screen and wrong for the other. The axis names the two rather than choosing, and the cost of the second is written where the choice is made.
to.offsetEnd: --slotted-table-sticky-offset-end, which is where the summary stops. It answers stickyTo page the way the offset answers it at the top: a page with a bar of its own across the bottom sets it once, and every summary under it stops above the bar.

sticky.columns: a cell whose sticky axis names start or end, resolved through inset-inline-start and inset-inline-end so a right-to-left document mirrors it
sticky.corner: A column header that is also a sticky column is both at once: it takes both offsets and the highest stacking step, stated once. With one step the header slides under the pinned column or the pinned column over the header.
sticky.print: Under @media print the scroll part releases its height and every sticky offset, so the platform's own rule — a thead repeats on each printed page — applies instead of being fought.

sort.written: on the sorted column header only, and removed from every other; the practice allows other and none as values and the family emits neither, because it sorts by one comparator and clears rather than saying nothing
sort.control: the column header's text wrapped in a button, which is what the APG's own sortable example does
sort.reorders: nothing. The rows are the consumer's own children, so the family holds the descriptor and the consumer applies it to its own array or its own query — the shape React Aria's sortDescriptor and Angular Material's matSortChange both take. A sorter per column is a data model, and a data model is the line between this family and data-grid.
sort.announce: the column and the direction, politely, through @slotted/core/live-announcer. aria-sort is a property, and a property that changes silently is a change no reader hears.
sort.indicator: a mask from --slotted-icon-chevron-down, turned a half turn for ascending. An unsortable column draws none; a sortable one draws it muted and reveals it on hover and focus, so no glyph is added to the foundation for one family.

columnControls.holds: the controls a column carries beside its name: a filter trigger, a column menu, a help hint, a unit switch
columnControls.layout: the name sits at the leading edge of the header and every control at the trailing one, so the header row is one line of triggers on the column boundaries — a column that both sorts and filters has two targets that never overlap
columnControls.control: drawn by this family, not taken from button: a library button at its smallest step is thirty pixels tall against a line of nineteen and a half, and its ghost hover is lighter than the band it stands on. The slot's button takes the expander's geometry, the header's own darker hover and the family's glyph size; the consumer keeps the behaviour.
columnControls.state: none. The family owns the place and the geometry; what a filter means, what it holds and what it leaves is the consumer's query, and filter-bar in wave 8 owns the typed rules.
columnControls.reason: Ant, PatternFly and Carbon all put a filter or a menu in the column header, and a listing screen is where every one of them is used. Declining the slot would have sent a consumer past the family for a button that has to sit inside a cell the family lays out: the sort control filled the header, and there was no room left for a second target. Found at the visual gate, on the question a listing screen asks first.

filter.shape: a trigger in the column-actions slot and a panel it opens: a search field, a checkbox that covers what the search left, the values with their counts, and a footer holding Clear and Apply.
filter.draft: The panel edits a draft. Nothing reaches the consumer until Apply, Escape and a press outside restore the set the panel opened with, and Clear empties the draft rather than the value. It is what Ant, AG Grid and Excel each do, and it is the difference between a filter and a list of checkboxes: a reader ticking four values fires one query, not four.
filter.search: shown once there are searchThreshold values or more, and it narrows on a fold that ignores case and diacritics. The covering checkbox then covers exactly what the search left, which is the behaviour a reader who searched then pressed it expects.
filter.counts: optional, and the consumer's own: how many records carry a value is a fact about the query, not about the column.
filter.applies: nothing. The filter reports the set the reader chose and the consumer's own query keeps or drops the rows — the same division sort already records, and the line this family holds against data-grid.
filter.marks: data-filtered on the trigger and on the column header that holds it, so a column filtered elsewhere on the screen still reads as filtered, and the trigger states the count in its own accessible name.
filter.announces: the count the panel is left with after a search, through the live announcer, because a list that shortens under a reader who cannot see it says nothing otherwise.
filter.empty: a word when the search matches nothing, so the panel is never a blank box.
filter.composition: popover holds the surface, checkbox holds every square, text-field holds the search and button holds the two actions. This family holds the place, the draft and the wiring.
filter.reason: A listing screen filters, and every surveyed implementation that ships a table for one ships this: Ant renders the value list with Reset and OK, AG Grid the set filter with a search and select-all, PatternFly and Carbon put the control in the header. The first version of this family shipped the slot and left the panel to the consumer, and what a consumer writes in an afternoon is a checkbox list with no draft, no search, no covering checkbox and no announcement. The place was not the hard part.

selection.columnWidth: --slotted-table-selection-size, and it is stated rather than shrink-wrapped so a column pinned beside the chooser has a length to state. Shrink-wrapped the answer was forty-two pixels: a number nothing names, so a consumer stating the nearest round one pinned the identifier past the chooser and over the column behind it.
selection.key: the row's own value, required whenever the selection or the expansion is on
selection.range: Shift while pressing a row's checkbox selects every row from the anchor to that one; the anchor is the last plain press.
selection.selectAll: The header checkbox covers the rows in the DOM, is indeterminate while some of them are selected, and states the count it covers in its own accessible name. A selection over a whole result set is a decision only the consumer's query can make.
selection.forbiddenReason: Under the table role a row is not selectable, so the property would be a promise the role breaks. data-selected paints the row and the checkbox announces it, which is the division list-item already recorded.

value.reason: The union listbox settled on: three of four surveyed collections give single selection a scalar, and the array-always shape is what makes every consumer write value[0].

expansion.wiring: the expander is a button carrying aria-expanded and aria-controls, naming the detail row's id
expansion.closed: the detail row is not rendered while it is closed, so nothing is in the DOM that a reader is told about and cannot reach
expansion.detail: one tr holding one cell that spans every column, which is what keeps the row group valid without a second table

numerals.rule: a numeric cell is set in tabular figures, so a column of numbers lines up digit under digit — §12 asks for it by name
numerals.inference: numeric aligns the cell to the end unless align says otherwise. It runs one way only, and the consumer's explicit align always wins.
numerals.reason: Alignment and numerals are two facts: a number is set in tabular figures whichever way it is aligned, and a right-aligned label is not a number.

blockAlignment.axis: cellAlign on the table, blockAlign on a cell
blockAlignment.reason: A row is as tall as its tallest cell, so a one-line value beside a three-line one either sits with it or hangs above it. Carbon, AG Grid and Material each centre, and a table whose rows are one line cannot tell the two apart. start is the answer a table of paragraphs wants, and the cell that wants it alone is usually one — the actions pinned at the end of a tall row — so the table states it once and a cell overrides it.

text.wrap: the default: the value wraps, and an unbroken token — a hash, a URL, an identifier — breaks with overflow-wrap: anywhere rather than setting the column's width
text.truncate: one line ending in an ellipsis, with the whole value still in the DOM and reachable, which is the briefing's decision that truncation never removes content
text.nowrap: one line that is never broken, for a value a break would make wrong: a date, a code, a short identifier
text.requires: truncate needs layout fixed to have a width to truncate against, which the family states rather than leaving to be discovered

loading.first: with no rows to keep, the loader part draws skeleton rows — columns cells wide, rows deep — so the table's shape is visible before its content
loading.refresh: over rows already shown, aria-busy goes on the table and the body dims; every column width is held and nothing moves, because a reader looking at row forty does not want to be moved to the top
loading.reason: Carbon draws a skeleton and Ant dims what is there; they are two states rather than two opinions, and a family with one answer gets the other one wrong.

empty.span: every column, through the columns the root states
empty.reason: result-state already separates an empty set from a set a filter emptied, and its status axis holds both words. A second empty shape here would be a second answer to a question a family already answers.

wiring.aria-labelledby: nothing the family writes. A caption is the table's accessible name by the platform's own rule, visible or visually hidden, and an authored reference would restate what the browser already states. An instance with no caption names itself with aria-label, which is the consumer's.
wiring.aria-describedby: the consumer's own, passed through untouched
wiring.aria-sort: on the sorted column header, and on no other
wiring.aria-busy: true on the table while it is loading over rows already shown
wiring.aria-rowcount: on the table only when the consumer states a total larger than the rows in the DOM, which is what the practice requires: the property exists to say the DOM is not the whole set, and a complete table that wrote it would count itself twice
wiring.aria-rowindex: on every row of a table that writes aria-rowcount, and on none otherwise — the practice warns that setting it on some rows and not others has devastating effects on assistive technology
wiring.aria-expanded: on the expander, with aria-controls naming the detail row
wiring.scope: col on a column header and row on a row header, which is what makes a screen reader repeat the record's name in each of its cells

keyboard.effect: moves to the next control the table holds: the scroll region while it overflows, then each sort button, selection checkbox, expander and consumer control in DOM order
activates the focused button: sorts the column, or opens and closes a row's detail
activates the focused button; on a row's checkbox it changes that row's selection
on a row's checkbox, selects every row from the anchor to that one
scrolls the region while it holds focus
scrolls along the inline axis, mirrored in a right-to-left document
scrolls the region by a view
scrolls the region back by a view
scrolls the region to its start
scrolls the region to its end

keyboardReason: The pattern defines no keyboard interaction, and that is the finding rather than an omission: a table is not a composite widget, so each control inside it is its own tab stop and every key above is the platform's. The one departure is the range gesture, which belongs to the checkbox the reader is already on.

Shift+Space.reason: A multi-row selection with no range is one press per row, which is what makes a reader select forty rows one at a time. Shift while pressing the checkbox — by pointer or with Space — is the gesture a file list, a mail client and React Aria's own table all use.
Shift+Space.cost: Shift+Space is the browser's own page-up in a scrolling region, so a reader whose focus is on a checkbox loses that shortcut for as long as it is. The scroll region keeps PageUp, which is the same movement under a key nothing else claims.

gridRole.reason: A grid is a composite widget with one tab stop and a cell cursor, and the four capabilities that need it — column resizing, virtualisation, multi-column sort and row activation — are all deferred to the same family. A table with twelve controls is twelve tab stops, which is what the APG says it is.

rowSelectedAttribute.composition: data-selected on the row, and the checkbox that announces it
rowSelectedAttribute.reason: aria-selected on a row under the table role is a promise the role breaks: the row is not a selectable widget, and a reader would be told about a state they cannot reach from where they are.

colcount.reason: aria-colcount and aria-colindex exist for a table that renders a subset of its columns, and this one never does — the consumer writes every column it wants shown. column-manager in wave 8 removes a column from the data rather than windowing over it.

rowActivation.composition: a link in the row-header cell, which is what Carbon, Primer and the HTML standard produce
rowActivation.reason: A tr cannot be an anchor, and under the table role a row is not a widget. Row-level activation is a grid behaviour and belongs to data-grid, which has the cell cursor that makes it reachable by keyboard.

multiSort.reason: The practice states that aria-sort has limited value on more than one header, because ARIA has no way to say which sort key came first. A second sorted column would be silent or a lie, and §12 puts multiple sorting in Data Grid's query model.

resize.reason: §12 puts width, min, max and resize in Data Grid's column model. It needs a per-column width state, a pointer gesture, a keyboard equivalent and a persisted preference — the four things that separate a grid from a table.

virtualization.reason: §2.10 makes virtualisation an optional capability of a collection, and a collection is what this family deliberately does not own: its rows are the consumer's own children. listbox holds the engine's windowing today and data-grid takes it for rows in wave 8.

pagination.composition: the footer part holds the control, and the table writes aria-rowcount and aria-rowindex around it
pagination.reason: The family is built and owns the page, the range and the keyboard. What this one supplies is the two halves pagination cannot: the place under the table and inside its frame, and the properties that say how large the whole set is when the DOM holds one page of it.

toolbar.reason: A search field and a filter control above a table are a toolbar, and filter-bar in wave 8 holds the typed rules. A toolbar built into the table would be a second answer to a question two families already answer.

headerSlot.composition: caption for the table's name, toolbar above it in the page's stack, action-bar in wave 7 for the bulk actions
headerSlot.reason: The footer had to be a part for two reasons that a bar above does not share: pagination sits flush under the last row with no ground of its own, and it must not scroll sideways with the table. A toolbar above stands on its own ground and the page's stack places it. The naming cost decided it: this anatomy already holds head for the thead, and head beside header is the pair a reader mistypes. If action-bar in wave 7 finds the seam is real, the slot is added there and the name is decided once.

batchActions.reason: Wave 7 builds it. This family supplies the selection and its count; where the actions are drawn — over the header, under the page, in a bar that appears — is the page's decision rather than the table's.

columnManagement.reason: §12 gives visibility, order and pinning their own Extended family in wave 8, and it is the family that can refuse to hide a mandatory column. This one honours the result: a column the consumer does not render is not there.

dragToReorder.reason: §3 makes drag-and-drop its own Extended module in wave 8, with the keyboard alternative that a gesture bolted onto this family would not have. The family exposes data-dragging for it and adds no gesture of its own.

cardLayout.reason: §12 names the recipe and forbids the shape PatternFly ships: "nunca converte células em cards sem labels". A card built from cells loses the column headers, and data-list is the family that carries a label beside every value.

size.reason: Carbon ships five sizes and Ant three. The theme restates the control scale at comfortable, compact and dense, and the row reads it; a family-owned step would be a second scale answering the same question, which is what description-list recorded.

clientSort.composition: const rows = useMemo(() => sortRows(data, sort), [data, sort]) — the descriptor applied to the consumer's own array
clientSort.reason: Ant's sorter per column and Material's MatTableDataSource both sort data the component owns. This family owns no data: its rows are children, and a family that reordered them would be reordering the consumer's JSX.

typedFilterRules.reason: The values of one column are this family’s; a rule set across columns is not. Operators, their serialisation, their validation and the bar that shows the rules together are filter-bar’s in wave 8, and a table that owned them would own the query — which is the line between this family and data-grid. A consumer who needs contains or between today puts their own control in the same panel: the parts are exported.

labelsReason: The eight words the family says, in one input rather than eight props: an application translates them once, and a family that spread them across the root would make seven of the eight a prop nobody sets. description-list and stepper group their own the same way, and none of them is a declared default — a default is a value a consumer overrides one at a time.

filter.scope: the filter, not the table: one column is filtered at a time and each filter holds its own set, so the three names sit on the part rather than on the root beside the selection that already uses them
